validation.note: Generated structured draft records; numeric-entry and complex-format keys require clinical/editorial completion before production exam use.

items.title: A client reports sudden flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like shadow over one eye. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Arrange same-day emergency ophthalmology evaluation, limit activity as instructed, and prepare for definitive treatment.
items.rationale: A curtain-like visual field defect suggests retinal detachment; prompt repair preserves vision.

items.title: A client 1 day after cataract surgery reports mild scratchiness but no severe pain or vision loss. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Reinforce eye-drop schedule, shield use, avoiding heavy lifting/straining, and urgent reporting of severe pain or sudden vision change.
items.rationale: Mild irritation may occur; severe pain or sudden loss of vision is not expected and needs urgent review.

items.title: A client has episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and fluctuating unilateral hearing loss. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Institute fall precautions during attacks, teach low-sodium plan if prescribed, and administer ordered symptom control.
items.rationale: Vertigo creates fall risk; dietary and medication management may reduce episodes.

items.title: A client receiving a potentially ototoxic medication reports new tinnitus and hearing difficulty. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client receiving a potentially ototoxic medication reports new tinnitus and hearing difficulty.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Report promptly, review drug levels/renal function and alternatives, and arrange hearing assessment.
items.rationale: Early tinnitus may precede permanent hearing loss from ototoxic medications.

items.title: A toddler has ear pain, fever, and bulging tympanic membrane. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A toddler has ear pain, fever, and bulging tympanic membrane.|response:Provide analgesia, assess age/severity and follow clinician plan for observation or antibiotics, and teach completion if prescribed.|rationale:Many cases are self-limited; treatment depends on age, severity, laterality, and follow-up reliability.
items.rationale: Many cases are self-limited; treatment depends on age, severity, laterality, and follow-up reliability.

items.title: A client has anterior nosebleed after dry air exposure and is hemodynamically stable. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Epistaxis|priority:Sit upright, lean forward, pinch soft part of nose continuously for 10–15 minutes, and avoid tilting head back.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Forward positioning prevents swallowing blood; sustained pressure is first-line for uncomplicated anterior bleeding.

items.title: A client receiving chemotherapy has painful oral ulcers and difficulty eating. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Oral mucositis|actions:Assess hydration/nutrition, provide gentle oral care and prescribed analgesia, avoid alcohol-based rinses, and monitor infection.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Mucositis compromises intake and mucosal barrier; gentle care and symptom management are essential.

items.title: A client receiving external-beam radiation has mild erythema in the treatment field. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client receiving external-beam radiation has mild erythema in the treatment field.|priority:Wash gently, avoid friction/heat and unapproved topical products, protect area from sun, and follow radiation-team instructions.
items.rationale: Radiated skin is fragile; gentle care reduces irritation and treatment disruption.

items.title: A vesicant chemotherapy infusion site becomes painful, swollen, and cool. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Extravasation can cause tissue necrosis; management is agent-specific and should follow protocol.

items.title: A client with cancer reports new severe back pain worse when lying down and with coughing. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: New progressive back pain in cancer may precede spinal cord compression.

items.title: A client with severe neutropenia has inflamed gums and oral soreness. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Use soft toothbrush or approved gentle oral-care method, avoid flossing if thrombocytopenic, and report ulcers/fever.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Gentle oral care reduces mucosal injury and infection risk; adapt to platelet count.

items.title: A dying client has noisy upper-airway secretions but no visible distress. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Reposition laterally, provide gentle mouth care, explain the sound to family, and use prescribed anticholinergic only if appropriate.
items.rationale: Noisy secretions often distress observers more than the patient; avoid deep suction that causes discomfort.

items.title: A client transitioning between opioid formulations has a new dose calculated from an equianalgesic table. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Opioid conversion safety|actions:Verify conversion with prescriber/pharmacist, apply incomplete cross-tolerance reduction when appropriate, and monitor sedation/respiration.|evaluation:Equianalgesic conversions are estimates; incomplete cross-tolerance and patient factors affect safe dosing.
items.rationale: Equianalgesic conversions are estimates; incomplete cross-tolerance and patient factors affect safe dosing.

items.title: A client with advanced disease asks whether choosing hospice means all care stops. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Explain hospice focuses on comfort and goals, continues symptom treatment and support, and review eligibility/services with hospice team.
items.rationale: Hospice changes the care focus, not the commitment to active symptom management and support.

items.title: A 62-year-old reports crushing substernal pressure radiating to the jaw for 25 minutes; skin is cool and ECG shows ST elevation in contiguous leads. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Activate emergency response, obtain/interpret 12-lead ECG, establish IV access, give aspirin if not contraindicated, and prepare for reperfusion.
items.rationale: Time-dependent myocardial injury requires rapid recognition and reperfusion; assess contraindications and follow ACS protocol.

items.title: A 71-year-old develops facial droop and unilateral arm weakness 40 minutes ago; bedside glucose is 108 mg/dL. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Activate stroke pathway, establish last-known-well time, check glucose, obtain urgent noncontrast head CT, and keep NPO pending swallow screen.
items.rationale: Rapid imaging distinguishes hemorrhage from ischemia; last-known-well guides reperfusion eligibility and swallowing precautions reduce aspiration.

items.title: A client with pneumonia is febrile, confused, BP 82/46 mm Hg, HR 128/min, lactate 4.2 mmol/L. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client with pneumonia is febrile, confused, BP 82/46 mm Hg, HR 128/min, lactate 4.2 mmol/L.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Escalate immediately, obtain cultures without delaying antibiotics, administer prescribed broad-spectrum antimicrobials and crystalloid, and reassess perfusion.
items.rationale: Hypotension and elevated lactate suggest septic shock; timely antimicrobials, fluid resuscitation, and reassessment are essential.

items.title: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting, deep respirations, glucose 486 mg/dL, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, and potassium 5.4 mEq/L. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting, deep respirations, glucose 486 mg/dL, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, and potassium 5.4 mEq/L.|response:Begin isotonic IV fluids, monitor potassium and ECG, initiate IV insulin per protocol after potassium assessment, and track glucose/anion gap.|rationale:DKA requires volume replacement and insulin; serum potassium may be elevated despite total-body depletion and can fall rapidly with treatment.
items.rationale: DKA requires volume replacement and insulin; serum potassium may be elevated despite total-body depletion and can fall rapidly with treatment.

items.title: An older adult with type 2 diabetes has profound dehydration, glucose 890 mg/dL, serum osmolality 342 mOsm/kg, and minimal ketones. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state|priority:Prioritize isotonic fluid replacement, frequent neurologic and electrolyte assessment, and insulin per protocol after initial fluids.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Severe hyperosmolality and dehydration dominate HHS; gradual correction and close monitoring reduce neurologic and circulatory complications.

items.title: A client with heart failure is acutely dyspneic, has diffuse crackles, pink frothy sputum, and SpO₂ 82%. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Acute pulmonary edema|actions:Sit upright, support oxygenation/ventilation, summon emergency assistance, and prepare prescribed diuretic/vasodilator therapy.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Pulmonary edema causes acute gas-exchange failure; respiratory support and rapid escalation take priority.

items.title: A client with acute kidney injury has potassium 6.8 mEq/L and peaked T waves on ECG. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client with acute kidney injury has potassium 6.8 mEq/L and peaked T waves on ECG.|priority:Initiate continuous ECG monitoring, escalate urgently, prepare IV calcium for membrane stabilization and potassium-shifting/removal therapies as prescribed.
items.rationale: ECG changes indicate cardiac toxicity; calcium stabilizes the myocardium while other therapies lower serum potassium.

items.title: A client receiving loop diuretics has weakness, potassium 2.7 mEq/L, and flattened T waves. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Hypokalemia increases dysrhythmia risk; IV potassium must never be given by IV push.

items.title: A postoperative client has urine output 15 mL/hr for 3 hours and creatinine rising from 0.9 to 2.1 mg/dL. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Oliguria and rising creatinine indicate impaired renal function requiring prompt evaluation of reversible causes.

items.title: A client with COPD has increased work of breathing, wheezing, and SpO₂ 86% on room air; baseline target is 88–92%. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Titrate controlled oxygen to the prescribed target, administer bronchodilators, assess for fatigue, and obtain blood gas as ordered.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Controlled oxygen and bronchodilation improve hypoxemia/airflow while monitoring for hypercapnia and respiratory failure.

items.title: A 19-year-old has severe wheezing, accessory muscle use, and speaks only one word at a time. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Treat as severe exacerbation: urgent escalation, inhaled short-acting bronchodilator, systemic corticosteroid, oxygen, and reassessment.
items.rationale: Inability to speak full sentences and accessory muscle use indicate severe airflow obstruction.

items.title: A postoperative client develops sudden pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, dyspnea, and SpO₂ 88%. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Pulmonary embolism|actions:Escalate immediately, support oxygenation, assess hemodynamic stability, and prepare for diagnostic evaluation and anticoagulation if prescribed.|evaluation:Acute dyspnea and pleuritic pain after surgery raise concern for PE; instability requires emergency response.
items.rationale: Acute dyspnea and pleuritic pain after surgery raise concern for PE; instability requires emergency response.

items.title: A chest drainage system becomes disconnected from the chest tube while the client is coughing. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Restore a sterile water seal per facility protocol, keep the system below chest level, assess respiratory status, and notify the provider.
items.rationale: Maintaining a water seal limits air entry; never clamp a chest tube routinely because tension pneumothorax may result.

items.title: A client after central-line insertion develops severe dyspnea, hypotension, absent breath sounds on one side, and tracheal deviation. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Call emergency response and prepare for immediate decompression; provide oxygen and support circulation.
items.rationale: Obstructive shock with unilateral absent breath sounds is a life-threatening tension pneumothorax.

items.title: A client reports hematemesis and melena; BP is 86/52 mm Hg and HR 132/min. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Assess airway and perfusion, activate urgent response, establish large-bore IV access, prepare fluids/blood products, and trend CBC/coagulation.
items.rationale: Hemodynamic instability suggests significant hemorrhage; circulation and airway protection are priorities.

items.title: A client has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, lipase four times the upper reference limit, and persistent vomiting. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, lipase four times the upper reference limit, and persistent vomiting.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Provide prescribed IV fluids and analgesia, monitor respiratory/renal status and electrolytes, and advance nutrition as clinically tolerated.
items.rationale: Pancreatitis care emphasizes supportive treatment, hydration, pain control, and surveillance for organ dysfunction.

items.title: A client has abdominal distention, colicky pain, bilious vomiting, and absent stool/flatus. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client has abdominal distention, colicky pain, bilious vomiting, and absent stool/flatus.|response:Keep NPO, initiate prescribed IV fluids, monitor electrolytes and abdominal findings, and prepare for imaging/decompression.|rationale:Obstruction risks fluid shifts, ischemia, and perforation; avoid oral intake until evaluated.
items.rationale: Obstruction risks fluid shifts, ischemia, and perforation; avoid oral intake until evaluated.

items.title: A client with suspected perforated viscus has rigid abdomen, rebound tenderness, fever, and tachycardia. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Peritonitis|priority:Escalate urgently, keep NPO, obtain IV access, prepare broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgical evaluation.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Peritoneal signs may indicate perforation and sepsis requiring urgent source control.

items.title: A client with cirrhosis is newly confused with asterixis and elevated ammonia. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Cirrhosis with encephalopathy|actions:Assess airway and neurologic status, identify precipitating factors such as bleeding/infection/constipation, and administer prescribed lactulose.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Hepatic encephalopathy requires treatment of precipitants and reduction of intestinal ammonia.

items.title: A client with atrial fibrillation reports sudden severe leg pain; the foot is pale, cool, and pulseless. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client with atrial fibrillation reports sudden severe leg pain; the foot is pale, cool, and pulseless.|priority:Notify vascular team immediately, keep limb at neutral position, assess neurovascular status, and prepare for anticoagulation/revascularization.
items.rationale: The six Ps indicate acute arterial occlusion; rapid intervention preserves limb viability.

items.title: A client with a tibial fracture reports escalating pain despite opioids and pain with passive toe stretch. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early signs; palpable pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome.

items.title: After trauma, a client has hypotension, bradycardia, warm dry skin, and motor weakness below the injury. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Loss of sympathetic tone can cause hypotension and bradycardia; spinal precautions prevent secondary injury.

items.title: A client with traumatic brain injury develops decreasing level of consciousness, vomiting, and unequal pupils. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Escalate immediately, maintain airway and neutral head alignment, elevate head about 30 degrees if not contraindicated, and avoid hip flexion.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Neurologic deterioration and pupillary change suggest rising ICP and possible herniation.

items.title: A hospitalized client begins generalized tonic-clonic movements while in bed. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Protect from injury, lower bed, turn to side when possible, time seizure, do not restrain or place objects in mouth, and assess airway afterward.
items.rationale: Safety and airway protection are priorities; nothing should be placed in the mouth during a seizure.

items.title: A client has fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Meningitis|actions:Initiate droplet precautions promptly, notify provider, obtain cultures/diagnostics as ordered, and do not delay prescribed antibiotics.|evaluation:Suspected bacterial meningitis is time critical and requires isolation and prompt antimicrobial therapy.
items.rationale: Suspected bacterial meningitis is time critical and requires isolation and prompt antimicrobial therapy.

items.title: A client receiving chemotherapy has temperature 38.4°C and absolute neutrophil count 300 cells/mm³. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Treat as an emergency: notify provider, obtain cultures, initiate prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly, and avoid rectal procedures.
items.rationale: Fever with severe neutropenia can rapidly progress to sepsis; avoid mucosal trauma and delays.

items.title: Fifteen minutes after packed RBCs begin, a client develops chills, back pain, and fever. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Stop transfusion, keep IV open with normal saline using new tubing, assess vitals, notify provider and blood bank, and follow reaction protocol.
items.rationale: Stopping the transfusion prevents further exposure; do not restart the same unit.

items.title: Minutes after an antibiotic, a client develops wheezing, facial swelling, urticaria, and BP 78/40 mm Hg. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Give IM epinephrine promptly per emergency protocol, call for help, support airway/oxygenation, and prepare IV fluids.
items.rationale: Epinephrine is first-line for anaphylaxis with airway or circulatory compromise.

items.title: A postoperative client is difficult to arouse, RR 6/min, and pupils are pinpoint after IV morphine. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A postoperative client is difficult to arouse, RR 6/min, and pupils are pinpoint after IV morphine.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Support ventilation, stimulate and call for help, administer naloxone per protocol, and monitor for recurrent respiratory depression.
items.rationale: Respiratory depression is the immediate threat; naloxone may wear off before the opioid.

items.title: A client 18 hours after last alcohol use has tremors, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and visual hallucinations. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client 18 hours after last alcohol use has tremors, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and visual hallucinations.|response:Initiate withdrawal assessment protocol, institute seizure/fall precautions, administer prescribed benzodiazepine, and give thiamine as ordered.|rationale:Withdrawal can progress to seizures or delirium tremens; benzodiazepines are first-line and thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy.
items.rationale: Withdrawal can progress to seizures or delirium tremens; benzodiazepines are first-line and thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy.

items.title: A client taking warfarin reports black stools and dizziness; INR is 5.8 and BP is 94/60 mm Hg. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Warfarin-associated bleeding|priority:Hold warfarin, assess hemodynamics, notify provider urgently, obtain CBC/type and screen, and prepare reversal therapy as prescribed.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Melena with supratherapeutic INR indicates potentially serious bleeding requiring stabilization and reversal assessment.

items.title: A client receiving unfractionated heparin has platelets fall from 220,000 to 88,000/mm³ on day 6. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia|actions:Stop all heparin products, notify provider, avoid platelet transfusion unless specifically indicated, and anticipate a non-heparin anticoagulant.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: A greater than 50% platelet fall in the typical time window suggests HIT, a prothrombotic immune reaction.

items.title: An older adult taking digoxin reports nausea and yellow vision; pulse is 48/min and potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:An older adult taking digoxin reports nausea and yellow vision; pulse is 48/min and potassium is 3.0 mEq/L.|priority:Hold dose, obtain ECG and digoxin/electrolyte levels, notify provider, and anticipate toxicity management.
items.rationale: Bradycardia, visual changes, and hypokalemia increase concern for digoxin toxicity.

items.title: A client with type 1 diabetes is prescribed rapid-acting insulin before meals; the meal tray is delayed. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin can cause hypoglycemia if food is delayed or unavailable.

items.title: A client receiving magnesium sulfate has RR 10/min, absent patellar reflexes, and urine output 20 mL/hr. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Respiratory depression and absent reflexes indicate magnesium toxicity; calcium gluconate is the antidote.

items.title: A client taking lithium develops vomiting, coarse tremor, ataxia, and confusion after several days of diarrhea. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Hold lithium, obtain serum lithium and renal/electrolyte studies, notify provider, and assess hydration and neurologic status.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Dehydration and sodium loss reduce lithium clearance and can precipitate toxicity.

items.title: During rapid vancomycin infusion, a client develops flushing and itching of face and upper torso without airway compromise. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Pause infusion, assess airway and vital signs, notify provider, and restart more slowly if prescribed after symptoms resolve.
items.rationale: Rate-related histamine release can cause flushing; distinguish it from anaphylaxis and follow prescribed rate adjustments.

items.title: A client taking lisinopril develops tongue swelling and hoarseness. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:ACE inhibitor angioedema|actions:Stop the medication, activate emergency airway response, and prepare for airway management.|evaluation:ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema can rapidly obstruct the airway; airway protection takes priority.
items.rationale: ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema can rapidly obstruct the airway; airway protection takes priority.

items.title: A client taking metformin is scheduled for iodinated contrast and has eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73 m². The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Notify the prescriber/radiology team and follow protocol to withhold metformin around contrast and reassess renal function before restarting.
items.rationale: Renal impairment increases risk of metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis; follow current contrast and renal guidance.

items.title: A family member asks to press the client's PCA button while the client sleeps. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Explain that only the client should activate PCA, assess sedation and respiratory status, and reinforce safety.
items.rationale: PCA by proxy increases risk of oversedation because the client cannot self-limit doses.

items.title: A nurse prepares IV potassium chloride for a client with potassium 2.8 mEq/L. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Dilute and administer via infusion pump at prescribed rate after checking renal function and urine output; never give IV push.
items.rationale: Concentrated potassium can cause fatal dysrhythmias if administered rapidly.

items.title: A client taking long-term prednisone reports fever and has fasting glucose 220 mg/dL. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client taking long-term prednisone reports fever and has fasting glucose 220 mg/dL.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Assess for infection and hyperglycemia, teach not to stop abruptly, and discuss lowest effective dose/taper only as prescribed.
items.rationale: Corticosteroids suppress immune response, raise glucose, and require tapering after prolonged use.

items.title: A client receiving gentamicin reports tinnitus and has rising creatinine. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client receiving gentamicin reports tinnitus and has rising creatinine.|response:Hold dose pending urgent review, notify provider, and assess renal function and drug levels as ordered.|rationale:Aminoglycosides can cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; early symptoms warrant prompt evaluation.
items.rationale: Aminoglycosides can cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; early symptoms warrant prompt evaluation.

items.title: A client receiving phenytoin has nystagmus, ataxia, and slurred speech. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Phenytoin toxicity|priority:Institute fall precautions, obtain level and medication review, and notify provider before further dosing.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Nystagmus and ataxia are common signs of elevated phenytoin levels.

items.title: Before metoprolol, a client's HR is 48/min and BP is 90/54 mm Hg. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Beta blocker and bradycardia|actions:Hold dose according to prescribed parameters, assess symptoms and perfusion, and notify provider.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Beta blockers reduce heart rate and blood pressure; symptomatic bradycardia/hypotension requires review.

items.title: A client taking clopidogrel reports new black stools and weakness. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client taking clopidogrel reports new black stools and weakness.|priority:Assess for bleeding and hemodynamic compromise, notify provider urgently, and do not advise stopping long-term therapy without prescriber direction.
items.rationale: Clopidogrel increases bleeding risk; suspected GI hemorrhage needs urgent assessment.

items.title: An older adult is admitted with multiple medication bottles and cannot recall doses. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Multiple sources reduce omissions, duplication, and dosing errors during transitions.

items.title: Twenty minutes after birth, a client has heavy vaginal bleeding and a boggy fundus. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Uterine atony is a common cause of postpartum hemorrhage; rapid response limits shock.

items.title: A 34-week pregnant client has BP 168/112 mm Hg, severe headache, and visual spots. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Escalate urgently, institute seizure precautions, administer prescribed antihypertensive and magnesium sulfate, and monitor reflexes/respiration.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Severe-range hypertension and neurologic symptoms increase risk of stroke and eclampsia.

items.title: A pregnant client with preeclampsia begins a tonic-clonic seizure. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Protect airway and client from injury, position laterally when possible, call emergency response, and administer magnesium sulfate per protocol.
items.rationale: Maternal stabilization and seizure control are immediate priorities; avoid restraining the client.

items.title: A 32-week pregnant client has painless bright-red vaginal bleeding and a soft nontender uterus. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Placenta previa|actions:Avoid vaginal examination, assess maternal/fetal status, establish IV access, and notify obstetric team.|evaluation:Digital examination can disrupt placenta previa and cause catastrophic hemorrhage.
items.rationale: Digital examination can disrupt placenta previa and cause catastrophic hemorrhage.

items.title: A pregnant client has sudden abdominal pain, dark bleeding, uterine tenderness, and frequent contractions. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Escalate immediately, assess maternal circulation and fetal status, establish IV access, and prepare for urgent delivery if indicated.
items.rationale: Painful bleeding and uterine tenderness suggest abruption with risk of maternal hemorrhage and fetal compromise.

items.title: After membrane rupture, fetal heart rate falls to 70/min and the cord is visible at the introitus. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Call emergency obstetric response, use a gloved hand to lift presenting part off cord, position knee-chest/Trendelenburg, and prepare for immediate birth.
items.rationale: Relieving cord compression preserves fetal oxygenation while expediting delivery.

items.title: During oxytocin infusion, recurrent late decelerations occur with contractions. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Stop oxytocin, reposition laterally, increase IV fluids as appropriate, assess maternal BP, and notify obstetric provider.
items.rationale: Late decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency; reduce uterine stimulation and improve perfusion.

items.title: After delivery of the fetal head, the shoulders fail to deliver and the turtle sign appears. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:After delivery of the fetal head, the shoulders fail to deliver and the turtle sign appears.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Call for help and assist with McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure; never apply fundal pressure.
items.rationale: Shoulder dystocia requires maneuvers that widen pelvic outlet and release impacted shoulder; fundal pressure worsens impaction.

items.title: An infant of a diabetic mother is jittery at 1 hour of life; bedside glucose is 32 mg/dL. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:An infant of a diabetic mother is jittery at 1 hour of life; bedside glucose is 32 mg/dL.|response:Follow neonatal hypoglycemia protocol: feed promptly if stable and able, recheck glucose, and give dextrose gel/IV glucose as indicated.|rationale:Jitteriness may signal hypoglycemia; prompt treatment prevents neurologic injury.
items.rationale: Jitteriness may signal hypoglycemia; prompt treatment prevents neurologic injury.

items.title: A term newborn has grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, and central cyanosis. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Newborn respiratory distress|priority:Call neonatal team, maintain warmth, support airway/oxygenation, and monitor preductal saturation.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Grunting and retractions indicate respiratory distress requiring prompt stabilization.

items.title: Two days after cesarean birth, a client has fever, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Postpartum endometritis|actions:Notify provider, obtain ordered cultures, administer prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics, and monitor for sepsis.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Postpartum fever with uterine tenderness and malodorous lochia suggests uterine infection.

items.title: An unsensitized Rh-negative client delivers an Rh-positive infant. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:An unsensitized Rh-negative client delivers an Rh-positive infant.|priority:Administer Rh(D) immune globulin within the recommended postpartum window and assess need for additional dosing based on fetomaternal hemorrhage testing.
items.rationale: Rh immune globulin prevents maternal sensitization and future hemolytic disease.

items.title: A client at 30 weeks has regular contractions and cervical change. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Corticosteroids improve fetal lung maturity; tocolysis may allow time for treatment when safe.

items.title: A breastfeeding client has unilateral breast erythema, fever, and flu-like symptoms. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Milk removal supports recovery; untreated bacterial infection may progress to abscess.

items.title: A 4-year-old has high fever, drooling, tripod posture, and muffled voice. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Keep child calm and upright, avoid throat inspection or tongue depressor, and summon airway-capable emergency team.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Manipulating the airway can precipitate complete obstruction in suspected epiglottitis.

items.title: A 2-year-old has barking cough, inspiratory stridor at rest, and suprasternal retractions. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Keep child calm, provide prescribed corticosteroid and nebulized epinephrine for moderate/severe symptoms, and monitor after treatment.
items.rationale: Stridor at rest indicates significant upper-airway narrowing; nebulized epinephrine has temporary effect and requires observation.

items.title: An 8-month-old with RSV has nasal congestion, poor feeding, RR 62/min, and mild retractions. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Bronchiolitis|actions:Assess work of breathing and hydration, suction nasal secretions, provide oxygen if indicated, and support hydration.|evaluation:Bronchiolitis treatment is primarily supportive; nasal suction can improve feeding and breathing.
items.rationale: Bronchiolitis treatment is primarily supportive; nasal suction can improve feeding and breathing.

items.title: A toddler has vomiting and diarrhea, dry mucosa, sunken eyes, and capillary refill 4 seconds. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Assess severity and perfusion, begin oral rehydration if mild/moderate and able, or isotonic IV bolus for shock/severe dehydration per protocol.
items.rationale: Rehydration route depends on perfusion and ability to tolerate oral fluids.

items.title: A child has 6 days of fever, bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, rash, and swollen hands. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Notify provider promptly and anticipate IV immunoglobulin and aspirin therapy with cardiac evaluation.
items.rationale: Early treatment reduces risk of coronary artery aneurysm.

items.title: A 10-month-old has episodic severe crying, draws knees to chest, vomits, and passes currant-jelly stool. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Keep NPO, establish IV access, monitor perfusion, and prepare for ultrasound and air/contrast enema reduction.
items.rationale: Intermittent pain and bloody mucus stool suggest intussusception; enema may be diagnostic and therapeutic.

items.title: A 5-week-old has projectile nonbilious vomiting, hunger after emesis, and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A 5-week-old has projectile nonbilious vomiting, hunger after emesis, and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Correct fluid and electrolyte deficits before surgical pyloromyotomy; monitor weight and urine output.
items.rationale: Persistent gastric losses cause dehydration and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; stabilize before surgery.

items.title: An infant with tetralogy of Fallot becomes cyanotic and irritable during feeding. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:An infant with tetralogy of Fallot becomes cyanotic and irritable during feeding.|response:Place infant in knee-chest position, provide oxygen, calm infant, and summon provider/emergency assistance.|rationale:Knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance and can reduce right-to-left shunting.
items.rationale: Knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance and can reduce right-to-left shunting.

items.title: A child with sickle cell disease has fever, chest pain, cough, and new pulmonary infiltrate. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Sickle cell acute chest syndrome|priority:Escalate urgently, provide oxygen if hypoxemic, initiate prescribed antibiotics/analgesia, encourage incentive spirometry, and prepare transfusion evaluation.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Acute chest syndrome is life-threatening and requires prompt supportive and disease-specific care.

items.title: A 20-month-old has a generalized seizure lasting 2 minutes during fever and is now drowsy but breathing. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Febrile seizure|actions:Protect airway and safety, time the event, assess recovery and glucose as indicated, and educate caregiver after evaluation.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Brief generalized febrile seizures are often self-limited; airway safety and assessment for cause are essential.

items.title: A child has fever, lethargy, hypotension, and a rapidly spreading nonblanching petechial rash. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A child has fever, lethargy, hypotension, and a rapidly spreading nonblanching petechial rash.|priority:Initiate droplet precautions, activate sepsis response, obtain cultures without delaying antibiotics, and support circulation.
items.rationale: Meningococcal sepsis can progress rapidly; isolation and immediate treatment are critical.

items.title: A 3-year-old has bruises in different healing stages and an injury explanation inconsistent with developmental ability. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Inconsistent history and patterned injuries require safeguarding and mandated reporting, not independent investigation.

items.title: A child has periorbital edema, 4+ proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and weight gain. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Protein loss causes hypoalbuminemia and edema; infection and thrombosis risks require monitoring.

items.title: A school-age child develops cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, and hypertension 2 weeks after strep throat. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Monitor BP, fluid balance, renal function, and electrolytes; restrict sodium/fluid as prescribed and report severe hypertension.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis causes inflammation, hematuria, fluid retention, and hypertension.

items.title: A child with type 1 diabetes has fever and vomiting with glucose 280 mg/dL. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Continue basal insulin as directed, check glucose and ketones frequently, encourage fluids, and seek urgent care for persistent vomiting or moderate/large ketones.
items.rationale: Illness increases insulin needs; stopping insulin can precipitate DKA.

items.title: A hospitalized child with autism becomes distressed by alarms and unexpected touch. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Autism spectrum care|actions:Use predictable routines, simple concrete language, sensory accommodations, caregiver input, and advance warning before procedures.|evaluation:Individualized communication and sensory support reduce distress and improve cooperation.
items.rationale: Individualized communication and sensory support reduce distress and improve cooperation.

items.title: A client says, “I have a plan to take all my pills tonight,” and has access to medications. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Maintain continuous observation, remove access to means, initiate immediate safety precautions, and notify mental health/emergency team.
items.rationale: Specific plan, intent, and access indicate imminent risk requiring immediate protection.

items.title: A client with bipolar disorder has slept 2 hours in 3 days, speaks rapidly, and spends impulsively. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Reduce stimulation, set clear limits, support hydration/nutrition and sleep, and administer prescribed mood-stabilizing treatment.
items.rationale: A structured low-stimulation environment reduces escalation and supports physiologic needs.

items.title: A client reports voices commanding them to harm a roommate. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Assess command content, intent, and ability to resist; protect potential targets, maintain observation, and notify team immediately.
items.rationale: Command hallucinations with potential harm require direct risk assessment and immediate safety planning.

items.title: A client experiencing sudden intense fear has palpitations, trembling, and hyperventilation; medical causes are being assessed. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client experiencing sudden intense fear has palpitations, trembling, and hyperventilation; medical causes are being assessed.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Remain with client, use calm brief statements, reduce stimuli, and coach slow breathing after ensuring medical stability.
items.rationale: Presence and simple grounding reduce panic; do not dismiss symptoms before excluding medical causes.

items.title: A client beginning lithium asks how to prevent toxicity during hot weather. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client beginning lithium asks how to prevent toxicity during hot weather.|response:Maintain consistent fluid and sodium intake, avoid dehydration, attend serum-level/renal monitoring, and contact provider for vomiting or diarrhea.|rationale:Fluid and sodium depletion can raise lithium concentrations and cause toxicity.
items.rationale: Fluid and sodium depletion can raise lithium concentrations and cause toxicity.

items.title: A client taking sertraline starts linezolid and develops agitation, diaphoresis, hyperreflexia, and fever. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Serotonin syndrome|priority:Stop serotonergic agents pending urgent review, obtain emergency assessment, and support cooling/fluids as prescribed.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Serotonin toxicity can be life-threatening; medication interaction and neuromuscular findings are key clues.

items.title: A client taking haloperidol has fever 40°C, severe rigidity, confusion, and autonomic instability. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Neuroleptic malignant syndrome|actions:Stop antipsychotic, initiate emergency medical response, provide supportive cooling/hydration, and anticipate prescribed specific therapy.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: NMS is a life-threatening reaction requiring immediate discontinuation and supportive management.

items.title: A client admitted after heavy alcohol use is tremulous and has a history of withdrawal seizure. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client admitted after heavy alcohol use is tremulous and has a history of withdrawal seizure.|priority:Use validated withdrawal scale, institute seizure precautions, administer prescribed benzodiazepine, and give thiamine before or with glucose when feasible.
items.rationale: Prior withdrawal seizure increases risk of complicated withdrawal; thiamine reduces Wernicke risk.

items.title: A severely malnourished client begins nutritional rehabilitation and develops weakness; phosphate falls to 1.2 mg/dL. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Refeeding syndrome causes dangerous intracellular electrolyte shifts, especially hypophosphatemia.
